newsitem.title: JAPAN: Outlook seen mixed for Japan waste-disposal stocks.
newsitem.headline: Outlook seen mixed for Japan waste-disposal stocks.

text.p: Expectations that Japan will tighten regulations covering highly toxic dioxin emissions attracted investors to makers of environmentally friendly waste disposal systems on Thursday, briefly sending their shares to their highest levels this year.

But the shares later slipped to end at or below their starting levels for the day and analysts said that, while the sector was likely to be supported by a global trend towards stricter toxic waste disposal rules, stiff competition in the sector meant the outlook was not wholly positive.
Incinerator makers Takuma Co Ltd and HEC Corp, and air filter manufacturer Nihon Spindle Mfg Co Ltd all hit new highs for 1997 in Thursday's trade.
But Takuma closed flat at 1,570 yen after rising to 1,590, HEC ended down 10 yen at 1,680 after hitting 1,780, and Nihon Spindle ended 23 yen lower at 490 after reaching 532.
Ebara Corp, a leading manufacturer of pumps and air blowers used in the disposal of industrial waste, jumped to a new 1997 high of 1,810 on Wednesday but closed 40 yen lower at 1,750 on Thursday.

Brokers said speculative buying of such issues was fuelled by expectations that an Environment Agency committee would decide later this month to recommend controls on dioxin emissions from industrial incinerators.
Dioxin is a highly toxic by-product of some industrial processes and is known to cause of wide range of diseases, including cancer.
Some brokers said the sector attracted investors who expect it to benefit from a focus on global environmental problems at the Group of Seven (G7) meeting in Denver later this month.
They added, however, that while the outlook for the companies was generally positive, it was clouded by the fierce competition in the sector and strong opposition to the siting of new incinerators.
"We can't be too optimistic," said Nobuaki Okimoto, an analyst at Nikko Research Center. "They will need to cut prices given the tough competition and this will affect their profits."
Kazuyuki Tone, environmental equipment analyst at Yamaichi Research Institute of Securities & Economics, said that the expected regulations would benefit incinerator makers.
"But in the near term, the outlook is for a tug of war between the benefits and strong protests against operations of the incinerators," he said.
Nikko's Okimoto said it was also possible that municipal bodies operating industrial incinerators would look at other ways of disposing of rubbish.
